passages.happening:
Paul comes to Derbe and then to Lystra. There he finds a disciple named Timothy, “the son of a believing Jewish woman and a Greek father” (verse 1). The believers in Lystra and Iconium speak well of him (verse 2).

Paul wants Timothy to come with him, so he circumcises him “on account of the Jews in that area, for they all knew that his father was a Greek” (verse 3). As they go from town to town, they hand on the decisions of the apostles and elders in Jerusalem (verse 4). “So the churches were strengthened in the faith and grew daily in numbers” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Lystra is the town where Paul was stoned and left for dead on his first trip (14:19). Timothy may have seen it happen. Now he joins the man the crowd tried to kill.

Timothy came from a mixed home. His mother was a Jewish believer, and his father was ‘a Greek’, which here means a Gentile. Paul later reminds Timothy of the faith that ‘first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice’ (2 Timothy 1:5), and says that from childhood Timothy had known the holy Scriptures (2 Timothy 3:15). He had a believing mother and grandmother, and he had not been circumcised.

Was Timothy counted a Jew? The later Jewish rule that a child of a Jewish mother is Jewish is written in the Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teaching put in writing around AD 200. Scholars argue over whether that rule was already held in Paul's day. Luke's own words show what mattered to the local Jews: ‘they all knew that his father was a Greek’. To them Timothy was a son of a Jewish mother who had been left uncircumcised, and that would have closed synagogue doors to him.

Then, from town to town, Paul hands on the Jerusalem letter of chapter 15, which told Gentile believers they need not be circumcised. The same Paul circumcises Timothy. That is the puzzle the note below faces.
passages.ot:
Circumcision went back to God's covenant with Abraham, and it was for every boy of the household: “every male must be circumcised when he is eight days old” (Genesis 17:12). Timothy, son of a Jewish mother, had never had it done.

Timothy's mother and grandmother had taught him the Scriptures, the Old Testament, from childhood. They did what the Law asked of every parent: to teach God's words “diligently to your children” (Deuteronomy 6:7).
passages.hard:
Why did Paul circumcise Timothy, so soon after the council said Gentiles need not be circumcised? And how does it fit with Paul's own letters? In Galatians he says that at Jerusalem “not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek” (Galatians 2:3). And he warns the Galatians, “if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all” (Galatians 5:2). On the face of it, Acts 16:3 seems to go against both.

Most readers answer that the cases differ. Titus was a Gentile, and some were pressing for his circumcision as if it were needed for salvation; to give in would have denied the gospel. The Galatians were Gentiles being told the same thing. Timothy was the son of a Jewish mother, and his circumcision was not about being saved. It was about opening doors among Jews, so that he could go with Paul into the synagogues. Paul wrote, “To the Jews I became like a Jew, to win the Jews” (1 Corinthians 9:20). He also wrote, “Was a man already circumcised when he was called? He should not become uncircumcised” (1 Corinthians 7:18): Jewish practice was not wrong for Jews, as long as no one made it the price of salvation.

Some scholars are not convinced. They doubt that the Paul of Galatians would have done this, and think Luke has shown Paul as more ready to give way to Jewish custom than he was. Others answer that Paul's letters always separate two things: circumcision demanded as a condition of salvation, which he fought, and Jewish practice kept freely, which he allowed. The book page's part ‘Acts and Paul's letters’ sets out this question with the others, and these notes do not settle it.
passages.asks: Paul fought hard so that Gentiles would not be forced into circumcision, and then asked Timothy to accept it freely, so that more people could hear. Ask where you insist on your freedom, and where you might give it up for someone else's sake. And notice Timothy's mother and grandmother. Ask who taught you the Scriptures, and whom you are teaching now.

passages.t: ‘Come over to Macedonia and help us’
passages.happening:
The Holy Spirit stops Paul and his companions from speaking the word in the province of Asia, so they travel through the region of Phrygia and Galatia (verse 6). At the border of Mysia they try to enter Bithynia, “but the Spirit of Jesus would not permit them” (verse 7). So they pass by Mysia and go down to the port of Troas (verse 8).

In the night Paul has a vision: a man of Macedonia stands pleading with him, “Come over to Macedonia and help us” (verse 9). “As soon as Paul had seen the vision, we got ready to leave for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Asia here is not the continent. It is a Roman province in the west of what is now Turkey, with Ephesus as its great city. Bithynia lay to the north, by the Black Sea. Twice Paul plans a route, and twice the way is shut. Luke does not say how the Spirit stopped them: by a prophet's word, by events, or by an inner certainty. He says only that it was the Spirit, and in verse 7 he calls him ‘the Spirit of Jesus’, a way of speaking that ties the Spirit closely to the risen Lord.

Later Paul teaches in Ephesus for two years, ‘so that everyone who lived in the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord’ (19:10). The ‘no’ was a ‘not yet’.

Troas was a port near the site of old Troy, on the coast facing Macedonia. Macedonia lay across the Aegean Sea, in what is now northern Greece. Crossing it meant taking the good news into a new province, and, as later readers have noticed, into Europe, though no one at the time would have thought of it in those words.

Then a small word changes. Luke has been writing ‘they’. Now he writes ‘we got ready to leave’. This is the first of the ‘we’ passages in Acts. Many readers take them in the plain way: the writer was there, travelling with Paul. Others think he used a diary kept by someone who was there. The book page sets out the views.

‘Concluding that God had called us.’ The vision did not come with a plan. Paul and his companions talked it over and drew a conclusion together. Guidance came through a vision, and through careful thinking about it.
passages.ot:
God often led his people by closing one road and opening another. When Israel left Egypt, “God did not lead them along the road through the land of the Philistines, though it was shorter” (Exodus 13:17). And God spoke to his servants in visions of the night, as he told Moses: “If there is a prophet among you, I, the LORD, will reveal Myself to him in a vision” (Numbers 12:6).

The cry ‘help us’ from a foreign land fits the prophets' hope that the nations would come looking for the God of Israel: “Many peoples will come and say, ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD’” (Isaiah 2:3).
passages.asks: Paul's plans were blocked twice before the right road opened, and he did not know why at the time. Ask whether a closed door in your life might be a ‘not yet’ rather than a ‘never’. And notice how they decided: not on a feeling alone, but by talking together about what God seemed to be showing them.

passages.happening:
From Troas they sail straight to the island of Samothrace, and the next day to Neapolis (verse 11). From there they go inland to Philippi, “the Roman colony of Philippi, the leading city of that district of Macedonia”, and stay several days (verse 12).

On the Sabbath they go outside the city gate to the river, where they expect to find a place of prayer, and they sit down and speak to the women gathered there (verse 13). Among them is Lydia, “a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message” (verse 14).

She and her household are baptized, and she urges them, “If you consider me a believer in the Lord, come and stay at my house” (verse 15). And she persuades them.
passages.hearers:
Neapolis was the port for Philippi, on the great Roman road called the Via Egnatia, which crossed Macedonia. Philippi was a Roman colony. After a battle fought on its plain in 42 BC, Rome settled former soldiers there, and the city was proud to be a small copy of Rome, with Roman law and Roman officials.

In other towns Paul went first to the synagogue. Here Luke speaks only of ‘a place of prayer’ by the river, outside the gate, and a group of women. Philippi seems to have had few Jews, perhaps no synagogue building at all.

Lydia is one of the most vivid people in Acts. She came from Thyatira, a city in the province of Asia, the very province where the Spirit had not let Paul preach. Inscriptions found at Thyatira speak of a guild, or trade association, of dyers there. Lydia sold purple cloth. Purple was prized, and the finest purple was very costly, worn by the rich and the powerful. She was a businesswoman, probably of some means.

She was ‘a worshiper of God’. That means she was a Gentile who worshipped the God of Israel and met with Jews to pray, without having become a Jew. Readers often call such people ‘God-fearers’, like Cornelius (10:2).

And she was the head of a household. Luke names no husband. She may have been a widow, or unmarried; the text does not say. In the Roman world a household took in more than parents and children. It included slaves, freed slaves who still worked for the family, and others who lived under one roof. When Lydia believes, her household is baptized with her, and she opens her house to Paul and his friends. The first church in Philippi meets in her home (verse 40).

Notice the order: ‘The Lord opened her heart.’ Lydia was listening, and God was at work in her listening.
passages.ot:
Fine purple cloth marked wealth in the Old Testament too. The capable wife of Proverbs is dressed in it: “her clothing is fine linen and purple” (Proverbs 31:22).

Lydia's welcome to strangers follows a long line in Scripture. Abraham ran to bring three travellers into his tent and fed them (Genesis 18:1-8). And a household turning to God together has an Old Testament echo in Joshua's words: “As for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Joshua 24:15).
passages.hard:
‘She and her household had been baptized.’ Did that household include infants? Christians who baptize babies and Christians who baptize only believers both read this verse, and the jailer's household later in this chapter (verse 33), with care. These notes set out both readings and do not choose between them.

Christians who baptize infants, among them Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Presbyterian and Reformed churches, read household baptisms as part of a wider pattern. God's covenant with Abraham included his whole household, and the boys were given its sign as babies. Peter promised the Spirit to ‘you and your children’ (2:39). So when the head of a household believed, the whole household, children included, was brought into the covenant community and baptized. They note that Luke tells of whole households baptized more than once (here, verse 33, and 1 Corinthians 1:16), and that it would be strange if none of them had young children.

Baptists, and many other Christians who baptize only believers, answer that the text does not say there were any infants, and that in these same stories the whole household also hears and believes. The jailer's household hears the word (verse 32) and rejoices that it has ‘come to believe in God’ (verse 34). Crispus ‘and his whole household believed in the Lord’ (18:8). On their reading, baptism follows a person's own faith, and ‘household’ means those in the house who heard and believed.

The text does not tell us the ages of anyone in Lydia's house. The note on Acts 2:37-41 sets out the wider views of baptism. All these churches agree that Lydia and her household were baptized at once, as people who now belonged to the Lord.
passages.asks: A wealthy Gentile businesswoman listened by a river, and the Lord opened her heart. Then she opened her home. Ask whether your faith has reached your house: your table, your spare room, your money. And ask whether you are listening to God in the ordinary places where people gather to pray.

passages.t: An enslaved girl with a spirit
passages.happening:
One day, on the way to the place of prayer, they are met by a slave girl with a spirit of divination, “who earned a large income for her masters by fortune-telling” (verse 16).

She follows Paul and the others, shouting, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who are proclaiming to you the way of salvation!” (verse 17). She keeps this up for many days. At last Paul, greatly troubled, turns and says to the spirit, “In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her!” And the spirit leaves her at that very moment (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Say it plainly: this girl was enslaved, and she was being used. Luke tells us she ‘earned a large income for her masters’. She had more than one owner. They made money from her, and, as the next verses show, the moment the money stopped they cared nothing for her at all. She was a person treated as a business.

‘A spirit of divination’ is, in Greek, ‘a spirit of python’. The Python, in Greek stories, was the serpent that guarded the oracle at Delphi until the god Apollo killed it, and the word came to be used of people who spoke as if a god was speaking through them. Fortune-telling means claiming to tell the future. People in Philippi paid her owners to have their futures read.

What she shouted was, in a sense, true. But ‘the Most High God’ could be heard in more than one way in that city. Jews used the title of the God of Israel, and inscriptions show Greeks also using ‘Most High’ for Zeus or for an unnamed highest god. And ‘a way of salvation’ could mean many things to a crowd. Paul did not want the good news announced by a spirit that held a girl captive.

Paul ‘grew so aggravated’, Luke says. He was troubled, worn down by it day after day. When he acts, he does not speak to the girl but to the spirit, and he commands it in the name of Jesus Christ, not in his own power. The spirit leaves her at once.
passages.ot:
The Law of Moses forbade fortune-telling: “Let no one be found among you who sacrifices his son or daughter in the fire, practices divination or conjury, interprets omens, practices sorcery” (Deuteronomy 18:10). Isaiah asked, “When men tell you to consult the spirits of the dead and the spiritists who whisper and mutter, shouldn’t a people consult their God instead?” (Isaiah 8:19).

The title ‘God Most High’ is old. Melchizedek, king of Salem, blessed Abram “by God Most High, Creator of heaven and earth” (Genesis 14:19).

The Law also named the stealing and selling of people as a crime worthy of death: “Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death, whether he sells him or the man is found in his possession” (Exodus 21:16).
passages.hard:
What became of her? The text does not say. Luke tells us the spirit left her, and then he follows her owners, not her. We do not know whether she was set free from slavery, whether she joined the believers, or what her owners did to her once she could no longer earn them money. It is honest to admit that we do not know. Some later readers have imagined she became part of the church in Philippi, but Luke does not tell us so.

The scene also shows how ordinary slavery was in the Roman world. The Bible's own law named kidnapping and selling people a crime, and Paul counts ‘slave traders’ among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). The site's Honest Answer, ‘Why didn't the Bible just ban slavery?’, faces the wider question of slavery in the Bible honestly and at length.

Human trafficking is the buying, selling or holding of people for forced work or for sex. It is evil, and it still happens today. The girl in Philippi was used for profit by people who owned her.

A word for anyone who has been sold, traded, or forced to work or to do sexual acts by someone who controls them, or who is in that place now. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Her owners saw a source of money. Paul, at last, saw a person held captive by a spirit. Ask whom you see only for what they are worth to you: at work, in what you buy, in what you watch. Some of what is cheap in our world is cheap because someone is being used. And ask whether you would act for someone held captive, even when it costs.

passages.t: Beaten with rods and thrown into prison
passages.happening:
When the girl's owners see that “their hope of making money was gone”, they seize Paul and Silas and drag them into the marketplace before the authorities (verse 19). They bring them to the magistrates: “These men are Jews and are throwing our city into turmoil” (verse 20), they say, “by promoting customs that are unlawful for us Romans to adopt or practice” (verse 21).

The crowd joins the attack, and the magistrates order Paul and Silas stripped and beaten with rods (verse 22). After many blows they are thrown into prison, and the jailer is ordered to guard them securely (verse 23). He puts them in the inner cell and fastens their feet in the stocks (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Notice what the owners do not say. They do not say, ‘These men have cost us our income.’ They say, ‘These men are Jews’, and they are teaching customs ‘unlawful for us Romans’. A complaint about money is dressed up as a defence of Rome and of the city's way of life. It plays on two fears at once: of foreigners, and of strange religion. The charge says more about the accusers than about the Jewish people.

The ‘magistrates’ were the two chief officials of the colony. Their attendants, mentioned in verse 35, were called in Greek ‘rod-bearers’, known in Latin as lictors, who walked before the magistrates carrying bundles of rods, the sign of Roman authority. Beating with rods was a Roman punishment. Paul later wrote, “Three times I was beaten with rods” (2 Corinthians 11:25), and he reminded the Thessalonians of the ‘shameful treatment in Philippi’ (1 Thessalonians 2:2).

There was no trial. The crowd shouted, the magistrates acted, and the two men were stripped and beaten in public. Then the jailer put them in the inner cell, the darkest and most secure, and fastened their feet in the stocks, a wooden frame that held the legs apart and made it hard even to sit or sleep.
passages.ot:
The innocent beaten and imprisoned is an old story in Scripture. Jeremiah was beaten and put in the stocks by a priest for speaking the LORD's word (Jeremiah 20:2). Joseph was thrown into prison though he had done nothing wrong: “While Joseph was there in the prison, the LORD was with him” (Genesis 39:20-21).

The prophets warned against those who crush the weak for profit. Amos condemned those who “sell the righteous for silver” (Amos 2:6).
passages.asks: A complaint about lost money became a riot about foreigners and religion. Ask whether you have ever dressed up your own interest as a defence of your community or your country. And notice who paid the cost: two men, stripped and beaten without a trial, because they had set a girl free.

passages.t: Midnight: ‘What must I do to be saved?’
passages.happening:
About midnight Paul and Silas are praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners are listening (verse 25). Suddenly a strong earthquake shakes the prison's foundations. At once all the doors fly open and everyone's chains come loose (verse 26).

The jailer wakes, sees the doors open, draws his sword, and is about to kill himself, thinking the prisoners have escaped (verse 27). But Paul shouts, “Do not harm yourself! We are all here!” (verse 28).

The jailer calls for lights, rushes in, and falls trembling before Paul and Silas (verse 29). He brings them out and asks, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” (verse 30). They reply, “Believe in the Lord Jesus and you will be saved, you and your household” (verse 31). They speak the word of the Lord to him and to everyone in his house (verse 32).

That same hour he washes their wounds, and he and all his household are baptized without delay (verse 33). He brings them into his home and sets a meal before them, and the whole household rejoices “that they had come to believe in God” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Paul and Silas have backs torn open by rods and feet locked in the stocks. At midnight they are singing. And the other prisoners are listening. In a place of misery, two men are praising God, and everyone in the dark can hear it.

Why would the jailer draw his sword? Because a guard who lost his prisoners could expect to pay with his own life. Earlier in Acts, King Herod had the guards of an escaped prisoner put to death (12:19). The jailer thinks he is ruined and will die in disgrace, and he means to end his life first.

Paul stops him. ‘Do not harm yourself.’ The man who had locked them in the stocks matters to Paul. And no one has run. The doors are open, the chains are loose, and the prisoners stay.

‘What must I do to be saved?’ The Greek word for ‘saved’ can mean rescued from danger as well as saved by God. The jailer may first have meant, ‘How do I get out of this?’ Paul and Silas give the word its fullest meaning. Their answer is short: ‘Believe in the Lord Jesus.’ To believe in him is to trust him as Lord, the one who rules, and to rest your life on him.

Then they speak the word to the whole household, so everyone hears for themselves. And the man changes before their eyes. He washes the wounds his own prison had given them. He sets food on his table for prisoners. Hours earlier he was about to die. Now his house is full of joy.

‘You and your household.’ The note on verses 11-15 above sets out how Christians read household baptisms.
passages.ot:
Songs in the night run through the Scriptures. Job speaks of “God my Maker, who gives us songs in the night” (Job 35:10), and a psalm says, “at night His song is with me as a prayer to the God of my life” (Psalm 42:8).

The earth shaking at God's coming is the language of the Psalms: “Then the earth shook and quaked, and the foundations of the mountains trembled” (Psalm 18:7). And setting prisoners free is the LORD's own work: “The LORD sets the prisoners free” (Psalm 146:7). Isaiah's servant would come “to bring prisoners out of the dungeon” (Isaiah 42:7).
passages.hard:
The jailer was about to kill himself. Luke tells it in one sentence, and Paul's shout stops it.

A word of care. Some people come to a moment when everything seems lost, and ending their life seems the only way out. If that is you, please do not carry it alone. Tell God, and tell someone near you: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. If you have thought of ending your life, please reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service where you live. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Paul's first words to the jailer were, ‘Do not harm yourself.’ The night that looked like the end was the night his house was filled with joy.
passages.asks: Paul and Silas sang in the dark, and the prisoners heard. Ask what the people near you hear from you when things go badly. And the jailer's question is still the question: ‘What must I do to be saved?’ The answer has not grown longer. Believe in the Lord Jesus. Ask whether you have.

passages.happening:
At daylight the magistrates send their officers with the order: “Release those men” (verse 35). The jailer tells Paul they may go in peace (verse 36).

But Paul says to the officers, “They beat us publicly without a trial and threw us into prison, even though we are Roman citizens. And now do they want to send us away secretly? Absolutely not! Let them come themselves and escort us out!” (verse 37).

The officers report this, and the magistrates are alarmed to hear that Paul and Silas are Roman citizens (verse 38). They come and appease them, lead them out, and ask them to leave the city (verse 39). Paul and Silas go to Lydia's house, see the believers and encourage them, and then leave (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
Roman citizenship was a legal standing, not a nationality, and in the eastern provinces only a minority held it. It protected the body. A citizen was not to be flogged or bound without trial, and he could appeal against a magistrate's sentence. In Philippi, a proud Roman colony, the magistrates had broken Roman law in public, and they knew it. That is why they are ‘alarmed’.

Why did Paul not say so the day before? Luke does not tell us. In the uproar he may not have been given the chance, or not been heard. Later, in Jerusalem, he does speak up before a flogging: “Is it lawful for you to flog a Roman citizen without a trial?” (22:25).

Why does he insist that the magistrates come in person? Not for revenge. A secret release would leave a stain: two Jews, beaten as troublemakers, slipping out of town. A public escort by the magistrates themselves says they were wronged and innocent. That protected the small church Paul was leaving behind, which had to go on living in that city.

Before they leave, Paul and Silas go to Lydia's house. The church in Philippi now meets there: a businesswoman from Asia, a jailer and his household, and, perhaps, others whose names we do not know. Years later Paul wrote to this church, “I thank my God every time I remember you” (Philippians 1:3), and reminded them, “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).
passages.ot:
God's law demanded justice without favour or haste: “Show no partiality in judging; hear both small and great alike” (Deuteronomy 1:17). The magistrates had heard no one at all.

And the righteous man's name cleared in public has Old Testament roots. Joseph, falsely jailed, was brought out and honoured before all Egypt (Genesis 41:14, 41-43). The Psalms pray for the same: “He will bring forth your righteousness like the dawn, your justice like the noonday sun” (Psalm 37:6).
passages.asks: Paul used his legal rights, not to save himself pain, but to protect a young church. Ask how you use whatever standing you have: your position, your money, your voice. For yourself, or for people more exposed than you? And notice where the chapter ends: in Lydia's house, with the believers being encouraged. Even after a beating, Paul's last act in Philippi is to strengthen others.
